result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_planar()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph is planar. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L4314-L4393){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_planar() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} A planar graph can be embedded in a plane without any edge crossings. This method uses Euler's formula and necessary conditions to test planarity. For simple planar graphs with `n ≥ 3` nodes, the number of edges *e* must satisfy `e ≤ 3n - 6`. For graphs without triangles, the stricter bound *e* ≤ *2n - 4* applies. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph satisfies planarity conditions, `False` otherwise. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} This is a *necessary but not sufficient* test. Some non-planar graphs may pass this test. For complete planarity testing, specialized algorithms implementing Kuratowski's theorem would be required. However, this test will correctly identify many non-planar graphs efficiently. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Small, sparse graphs are almost always planar: ::: {#a7a6d476 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") ) graph.is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: `K_4` sits right at the edge-count bound for planarity (`6 edges = 3*4 - 6`), and is in fact planar: ::: {#5304a292 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(n=4) graph.is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: `K_5` exceeds that same bound (`10 edges > 3*5 - 6 = 9`), so this check correctly flags it as non-planar: ::: {#243f770e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(n=5) graph.is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Trees always satisfy the bound comfortably, since they have only `n - 1` edges: ::: {#61dd2e8e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree = ec.Graph(directed=False) tree.add_balanced_tree(k=3, h=4) tree.is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Grids are sparse enough to stay planar as well: ::: {#2a188435 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} grid = ec.Graph(directed=False) grid.add_grid_2d(rows=5, cols=5) grid.is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` True ``` ::: :::
